rationale: A wins because it knows where the edge of the facts is and stops there. Its strongest line, "A 22% drop in no-shows: what Mindbody's AI pilot proves and what it doesn't," turns the launch into a legitimate trade-data story without swallowing the company claim whole. B has sharper ambition, but "The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" is a loaded insinuation built on a fact pattern that only says Mindbody owns ClassPass and texts waitlisted members. That's a good question, not a pitchable angle yet.
gaps_in_A: "operator-focused reporter at a boutique-fitness or salon trade outlet" stretches the launch slightly; the product is for boutique fitness and wellness studios, while salons are only part of Mindbody's broader footprint.
"Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" is sound, but it needs competitor pricing or an executive willing to discuss retention before it becomes more than a smart business-software sidebar.
gaps_in_B: "studios get it whether or not they asked for it" is not in the update. Bundled pricing does not prove automatic rollout, consent, or forced adoption.
"the fitness industry has been guessing at for years" invents a market context. Maybe true, maybe not; the update does not give that history.
"The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" overstates the facts. The assistant texts waitlisted members; nothing says ClassPass inventory or prioritization is involved.
"that's a recognizable PE playbook" drags in private-equity strategy without proof. The update says take-private and bundled pricing, not margin engineering or retention targets.
